title: No-Go Theorem and Routes towards Cavity-Enhanced Superconductivity
abstract: Recent experiments reporting cavity-vacuum-modified superconductivity raise a fundamental question: under what conditions can vacuum electromagnetic fluctuations increase a superconducting transition temperature? Starting from a Ginzburg--Landau theory minimally coupled to a quantized cavity mode, we derive the cavity-induced renormalization of the superconducting free energy. This correction comprises a positive diamagnetic contribution and a negative paramagnetic exchange contribution. We prove that, in a passive cavity, the latter cannot exceed the former, establishing a no-go theorem: within minimal cavity electrodynamics, vacuum fluctuations suppress, rather than enhance, superconductivity. We then identify two routes beyond this constraint, both involving additional collective degrees of freedom. In the collective-mode route, a cavity-active excitation amplifies the attractive paramagnetic contribution. In the competing-order route, the cavity weakens an order that competes with superconductivity, thereby indirectly enhancing superconductivity. Together, these results turn the no-go theorem into a practical design principle: cavity superconductivity enhancement requires an additional cavity-coupled material mode that either strengthens paramagnetic exchange or suppresses a competing order.
summary: This theoretical paper investigates how coupling superconductors to electromagnetic cavities affects their critical temperature ($T_c$). It first proves that simple vacuum fluctuations suppress superconductivity (a no-go theorem). To achieve enhancement, the authors show that one must introduce additional coupled material modes—either through a collective excitation or by suppressing a competing order—making it a guide for designing superconducting devices using cavity QED principles.
main_problem: The primary question is determining the conditions under which vacuum electromagnetic fluctuations, mediated by a cavity, can enhance superconductivity (increase $T_c$).
main_result: A no-go theorem proves that minimal coupling to passive cavity modes suppresses superconductivity; enhancement requires introducing additional coupled material degrees of freedom.
method: The authors derive the effective superconducting free energy by integrating out the quantized cavity mode, leading to corrections involving diamagnetic and paramagnetic terms.
model_or_system: The system is a bulk superconductor described by Ginzburg-Landau theory ($\phi$), minimally coupled to quantized cavity modes ($A$). Enhancement mechanisms involve coupling to additional collective excitations or competing order parameters ($\chi$).
key_observables: Superconducting transition temperature shift ($\delta T_c$); the balance between diamagnetic and paramagnetic energy corrections.
important_parameters: Cavity frequency ($\omega_c$), material mode frequencies ($\Omega_X$), and the coupling strength of the additional degrees of freedom.
main_assumptions: The initial analysis assumes minimal coupling to a passive cavity. Circumvention requires introducing additional coupled modes (collective or competing order).
figures_summary: Figure 1 illustrates renormalization diagrams; Figure 2 shows $\delta T_c$ dependence on cavity frequency, peaking at resonance for the collective-mode route; Figure 3 shows enhancement/suppression for the competing order.
paper_structure: The paper first establishes the no-go theorem using minimal coupling. It then systematically explores two routes beyond this constraint: the collective-mode route and the competing-order route, showing how each can lead to enhanced $T_c$ near resonance.
why_interesting: This work directly bridges superconducting physics with cavity quantum electrodynamics (Cavity QED) by treating vacuum fluctuations as a tunable parameter. The identification of necessary additional coupled modes provides concrete design principles for enhancing superconductivity using optical cavities, which is highly relevant to AMO/Quantum Optics.
